video_title: Is there way more conventional geothermal than we thought?
gist: METADATA DISCREPANCY: the raw record is titled 'Is there way more conventional geothermal than we thought?' on the Volts channel, but the transcript contains no geothermal or energy content whatsoever — it is a live on-stage interview at the Odoo Experience conference in San Francisco between a host identified as Scott (NYU Stern professor, Prof G) and Stanford's Bill Burnett and Dave Evans, authors of 'Designing Your Life' and 'How to Live a Meaningful Life'. All insights below come from that actual conversation, which covers career design, the mechanics of a hiring market now gated by AI resume screening, the separation of money-making from meaning-making, and attribution of success to luck versus grit.

insights.claim: Burnett and Evans devote an entire chapter of their first book to how NOT to find a job — namely by applying — and argue the online application channel is now structurally broken because AI resume screening filters candidates before a human ever sees them.
insights.speaker: Dave Evans / Bill Burnett, Stanford educators
insights.so_what: If the application funnel is genuinely dead, the value migrates to referral and network-graph products rather than to job-board businesses that monetize application volume.
insights.quote: We got a whole chapter in our first book about how not to find a job, which is by applying.

insights.claim: Response rates on cold job applications run roughly three to five percent — one Stanford student hand-wrote 100 cover letters and resumes and received exactly three responses.
insights.speaker: Bill Burnett, Stanford educator
insights.so_what: A concrete conversion benchmark for the white-collar hiring funnel; any recruiting-tech product must clear this baseline to justify pricing.
insights.quote: I sent in a 100 resumes. I got three responses. I said, 'Well, then you're that's about average. It's three to five percent.

insights.claim: Burnett's explicit purpose for referral networking is now mechanical rather than social: a loose network connection exists to get a resume past the AI screening layer to where a human being will actually look at it.
insights.speaker: Bill Burnett, Stanford educator
insights.so_what: Reframes referrals as a filter-bypass mechanism — implying employee-referral and warm-intro tooling captures disproportionate value as automated screening spreads.
insights.quote: get your resume out of this AI, you know, screening system to the top of the layer where a human being looks at it

insights.claim: From inside Apple's hiring process, a single posted design role would draw 5,000 resumes within a minute, and the hiring manager got no additional time to screen them — a single verbal recommendation moved a candidate straight onto the interview list.
insights.speaker: Bill Burnett, formerly Apple
insights.so_what: Quantifies why applicant volume is worthless as a signal and why manager attention, not candidate supply, is the true bottleneck in hiring.
insights.quote: we post a thing for a designer. We get 5,000 resumes in a minute

insights.claim: Job seekers systematically mis-map the labor market: a Stanford career counselor found students believe the world consists of the companies that do on-campus recruiting, which is roughly 0.01% of companies on the planet.
insights.speaker: Bill Burnett, Stanford educator
insights.so_what: Explains persistent crowding into a tiny set of prestige employers — and the corresponding talent arbitrage available to firms that recruit outside that channel.
insights.quote: The students believe the world is the collection of companies that do on-ampus recruiting. That's 0.01% of the companies on the planet.

insights.claim: Two-thirds of US job creation comes from small and medium-sized businesses, meaning two-thirds of available roles sit outside the companies candidates can find via LinkedIn or trade press.
insights.speaker: Scott Galloway, host
insights.so_what: The structural argument for SMB-focused recruiting, payroll and software platforms — the demand is where the discovery tooling isn't.
insights.quote: twothirds of job creation is from small and mediumsiz business

insights.claim: Average starting salary out of NYU Stern's business school is now $212,000, and Galloway observes that when graduates complain about not getting a job, the actual complaint is that they cannot get the specific job they want.
insights.speaker: Scott Galloway, host
insights.so_what: A hard compensation benchmark for elite MBA talent, plus evidence that reported white-collar 'unemployment' distress at the top end is selectivity, not scarcity.
insights.quote: the average starting salary now at a business school is $212,000

insights.claim: Galloway's stated success function for job hunting and fundraising is endurance of rejection rather than talent or timing — he says he has never had an easy time raising money or finding a job even in the strongest bull economies.
insights.speaker: Scott Galloway, host
insights.so_what: A counterweight to the 'easy money' narrative around startup fundraising from someone who has done it repeatedly; useful calibration for founder expectations.
insights.quote: I've never had an easy time raising money. I've never had an easy time finding a job. I even in the biggest bull economies, I never thought it was easy.

insights.claim: Angela Duckworth, who wrote the book on grit, concluded that a failing school system's problem was not insufficient student grit but missing preconditions — teachers buying their own supplies, kids lacking hot lunch and breakfast — a direct rebuke of the resilience framing she is famous for.
insights.speaker: Bill Burnett, Stanford educator
insights.so_what: Undercuts individual-resilience explanations for underperformance in favor of structural inputs — relevant to how workforce and education interventions are evaluated.
insights.quote: Your school system doesn't work because not because the kids aren't gritty, because you aren't giving them the circumstances they need.

insights.claim: Evans argues the modern Western premise that one job should deliver income, fulfillment and world-improvement simultaneously is historically anomalous — for the overwhelming majority of human history money-making and meaning-making were separate activities.
insights.speaker: Dave Evans, Stanford educator
insights.so_what: A reframe that directly attacks the 'purpose-driven employer' value proposition companies use to justify below-market pay.
insights.quote: And meaning making and moneymaking don't have to be the same.

insights.claim: Evans frames work as three horizontal, not hierarchical, categories — jobs done for money, careers done for professional development, and callings done for missional fulfillment — and illustrates it with a heart surgeon who holds his role purely as a job and claims he is better at it precisely because he isn't emotionally invested.
insights.speaker: Dave Evans, Stanford educator
insights.so_what: A useful lens on talent retention: employees optimizing for 'job' will not respond to mission-based incentives, only to compensation.
insights.quote: You do jobs for money, careers for professional development, and callings for missional fulfillment and values realization. Most people stack those vertically.

insights.claim: Whether your interests happen to align with what the market currently rewards is luck, not merit — Evans contrasts a CS student working on AI for retail and enterprise software ('really convenient to be you right now') with a student wanting to make nature documentaries ('terribly inconvenient to be you right now').
insights.speaker: Dave Evans, Stanford educator
insights.so_what: A clean statement of sector timing as the dominant variable in individual career returns — the human-capital analogue of factor exposure.
insights.quote: You don't get to pick the you. You don't get to pick the universe you're in

insights.claim: 'Follow your passion' is dysfunctional advice because Stanford's Bill Damon found fewer than 20% of people have a singular identifiable passion — and most of that 20% names artistic pursuits that they are then told are not real jobs.
insights.speaker: Bill Burnett, Stanford educator
insights.so_what: A research-backed attack on the dominant career-advice frame, and an explanation for why passion-based employer branding fails on 80% of candidates.
insights.quote: Less than 20% of people have a singular identifiable passion.

insights.claim: Ten years after graduation, fewer than 20% of people are doing work connected to their college major, which Burnett summarizes as: a major is how you organize college, not how you organize your life.
insights.speaker: Bill Burnett, Stanford educator
insights.so_what: Weakens the case for major-specific degree pricing and supports the shift toward shorter, modular credentialing.
insights.quote: Major is the way you organize college is not the way you organize your life.

insights.claim: Following the pandemic and the Great Resignation, 52 million people left jobs looking for something better, and the feedback from those who found it didn't work split roughly 80/20 toward wanting impact over wanting fulfillment.
insights.speaker: Dave Evans, Stanford educator
insights.so_what: Names the dominant driver of voluntary quits as perceived impact rather than compensation or fulfillment — a specific lever for retention programs.
insights.quote: after the pandemic and then the great resignation, 52 million people walk off the job looking for something better

insights.claim: Evans argues both impact and fulfillment are dead ends as sole sources of meaning — impact usually fails and its glow is short-lived, while Maslow-style self-actualization is impossible because nobody can manifest more than a fraction of themselves in one lifetime.
insights.speaker: Dave Evans, Stanford educator
insights.so_what: A direct challenge to the impact-and-purpose vocabulary that dominates both employer branding and ESG-style personal positioning.
insights.quote: if impact which is a thing and you're not a thing.

insights.claim: The positive psychology movement's founding book 'Authentic Happiness' and its happiness equation have been largely debunked, and the field has moved to flourishing and thriving as the operative constructs.
insights.speaker: Dave Evans, Stanford educator
insights.so_what: A caution that widely-cited wellbeing frameworks embedded in corporate HR programs rest on partially retracted science.
insights.quote: there's a happiness equation and the book has largely been debunked as not particularly true

insights.claim: Burnett and Evans apply industrial design methodology to life decisions on the grounds that a person's future is an unknown thing about which you cannot get data — so you must build and test rather than analyze.
insights.speaker: Bill Burnett, Stanford educator
insights.so_what: The same argument used for lean product development, applied to human capital — a transferable heuristic for decisions where no historical base rate exists.
insights.quote: They're they're an unknown thing in the future and you can't get any data. So, you have to figure out how to design it.

insights.claim: Burnett's core claim from seven years at Apple is that building a prototype changes the set of possibilities itself — observers behind the glass immediately generate options nobody had conceived before the artifact existed.
insights.speaker: Bill Burnett, formerly Apple
insights.so_what: An argument that the option value of shipping a rough artifact exceeds the information value of further analysis — the case for fast, cheap experiments over research budgets.
insights.quote: As soon as you have a prototype, you change the world as possible.

insights.claim: Evans rejects the search for a singular purpose entirely: purpose should be an adverb rather than a noun, and the operative cycle is be-do-become, where each round of doing produces a new identity that redefines what to do next.
insights.speaker: Dave Evans, Stanford educator
insights.so_what: Reframes career transitions as expected iterations rather than failures — relevant to how firms structure internal mobility.
insights.quote: There is no figuring it out. There's only getting on with it.

insights.claim: Burnett's practical protocol for someone completely stuck is to set the bar low, clear it, and repeat — explicitly aligning with James Clear's Atomic Habits and pairing it with curiosity and small prototype experiments to build momentum.
insights.speaker: Bill Burnett, Stanford educator
insights.so_what: A low-cost intervention model that scales — relevant to how behavior-change and coaching products should be designed.
insights.quote: set the bar low, clear it, do it again, do it again, do it again

insights.claim: The compass exercise operationalizes meaning as coherence between three written artifacts — your inherited story, a workview answering why we work, and a lifeview of 250 to 500 words — on the research finding that you cannot connect a dot you have not articulated.
insights.speaker: Bill Burnett and Dave Evans, Stanford educators
insights.so_what: A concrete, repeatable diagnostic that has sold two million books — evidence of real willingness-to-pay for structured career-clarity products.
insights.quote: You can't connect a dot you've not articulated.

insights.claim: Galloway argues America captured 30% of world GDP growth from 1945 to 2000, and two-thirds of that accrued to the one-third of the population that was white, male and heterosexual — making demographic timing, not merit, the dominant driver of his own outcomes.
insights.speaker: Scott Galloway, host
insights.so_what: A quantified statement of how concentrated the post-war wealth cohort was — context for the political economy of current redistribution debates.
insights.quote: America 30% of the world's GDP growth 1945 to 2000 and twothirds of that was crammed into the one-third of the population that looks, smelt and felt like me.

insights.claim: Galloway's specific critique of the tech community is that it credits grit and character for its successes while blaming markets for its failures — a systematic attribution asymmetry.
insights.speaker: Scott Galloway, host
insights.so_what: A caution for evaluating founder and manager track records: separating skill from beta is the whole question, and the industry is structurally biased against doing so.
insights.quote: the tech community uh is very good at crediting their grit and character for their success and then blaming the markets for their failure

insights.claim: Galloway accuses the tech industry of pretending to care about the world while depressing teens to sell more advertising, and argues it would be more honest to state plainly that the current objective is money and economic security.
insights.speaker: Scott Galloway, host
insights.so_what: The mental-health externality framing is the core of the regulatory and litigation risk facing ad-funded social platforms.

insights.claim: Galloway's retrospective thesis is that money was the means and the actual end was meaningful relationships in the absence of economic anxiety — he pursued wealth sequentially, at the cost of his hair and first marriage, and says it was worth it.
insights.speaker: Scott Galloway, host
insights.so_what: An explicit defense of sequential rather than concurrent optimization — the opposite of the work-life integration orthodoxy, from someone who ran the experiment.
insights.quote: the money was the means but the ends was meaningful relationships with an absence of economic anxiety

insights.claim: Galloway cites that 75% of women say economic viability is central in a mate versus only 25% of men, and that in San Francisco men remain twice as likely to out-earn their female partner despite income parity holding until women have children.
insights.speaker: Scott Galloway, host
insights.so_what: The motherhood earnings penalty is the identified breakpoint in pay parity — the specific place policy or employer benefits would have to intervene.
insights.quote: 75% of women say economic viability is central to a mate. It's only 25% of men.

insights.claim: Galloway describes atheism as a practical performance unlock because it collapses the time horizon and eliminates fear of embarrassment, rejection, or taking a role beneath one's perceived status.
insights.speaker: Scott Galloway, host
insights.so_what: An unusual but concrete model for why some operators tolerate far more rejection and status risk than peers — a trait worth screening for in founders.
insights.quote: to not take risks and to be worried about what other people think about you is just such a waste

insights.claim: Evans points to the Gottman Institute's love lab — which videotaped couples for years to behaviorally identify the masters and disasters of partnership — as the empirically settled answer to mate selection, specifically values alignment and a shared image of the future.
insights.speaker: Dave Evans, Stanford educator
insights.so_what: Points to an observational-behavioral methodology that outperformed theoretical models — a general argument for measuring revealed behavior over stated preference.
insights.quote: We just need to observe what works and what doesn't.

insights.claim: The longest-running study of humans ever conducted, the Harvard adult development study spanning three generations and 75 years, produced the conclusion from George Vaillant that happiness is love, full stop.
insights.speaker: Dave Evans, Stanford educator
insights.so_what: The single most-cited longitudinal finding on wellbeing, and the empirical anchor for the episode's claim that relationships outrank achievement.
insights.quote: happiness is love. Full stop.

insights.claim: Evans's tested rule for durable partnership is that a healthy person must partner with a healthy person — defined as knowing your own baggage and having people in your life who will call you on it — with love as necessary but insufficient.
insights.speaker: Dave Evans, Stanford educator
insights.so_what: A screening heuristic that generalizes to co-founder selection: self-awareness plus a functioning accountability network beats chemistry alone.
insights.quote: be a healthy person who marries a healthy person for love. Love isn't enough, but if you don't have it, it's pretty tough.

insights.claim: Burnett relays his mother's explicit instruction not to design a life around children because the parenting window closes at 18 if you do the job correctly — the kids leave and do not come back.
insights.speaker: Bill Burnett, Stanford educator
insights.so_what: Names the empty-nest transition as a predictable, plannable identity shock rather than a surprise — a large and underserved demographic moment.
insights.quote: Don't design your life around your children. They don't last. Love them when you have them, but have something else in mind.

insights.claim: Evans reframes loss of purpose after children leave as success rather than failure — you did not lose your purpose, you completed it — prescribing a party, then grief, then attention to the next invitation.
insights.speaker: Dave Evans, Stanford educator
insights.so_what: A reusable framing for any completed mandate, including executives and founders after an exit.
insights.quote: You you didn't lose your purpose. You succeeded at it.

insights.claim: Evans's own example of a late-career pivot took roughly twenty years of small moves — his wife left a 40-year San Francisco art gallery career with no idea what came next, eventually inventing the role of 'letter midwife' and assisting 800 people in writing the essential letters of their lives.
insights.speaker: Dave Evans, Stanford educator
insights.so_what: A concrete data point on the realistic timescale of a genuine reinvention — two decades, not two years.
insights.quote: So, if you're stuck, just identify what you are drawn toward and make a move.
